A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ADAPT-Z research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, and detailed results tables, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting experiments across 13 datasets and three base models, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and experiments with different seeds.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds gradient-statistics analyses, deployment-efficiency measurements, and comparisons with PETSA and TAFAS.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the condition for starting historical-gradient computation and parameter updates from t >= k + b - 1 to t >= k + b. This changes the documented procedure by one timestep. The feature correction, dual-input adapter, losses, and updated parameter subsets remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 13 forecasting datasets. The added gradient, efficiency, and test-time-adaptation comparisons reuse existing datasets and forecasting tasks without introducing a distinct data domain or input scenario.

E2.justification: Appendix H and Table 10 add a substantive comparison against PETSA and TAFAS across six existing datasets and two backbones. These methods were not evaluated in v1. FSNet and OneNet appearing in v2's Table 2 are redisplayed comparisons already present in v1's detailed Table 7.

E3.justification: V2 introduces protocols for relating gradient RMSD/MAV to prediction error and measuring deployment time and GPU memory on ETTm1 and traffic. The existing forecasting splits, lookback, horizons, and base models are retained. Batchwise prediction is newly disclosed rather than established as a changed experimental setting.

E4.justification: Section 4.3.3 adds an analysis testing whether gradient stability or magnitude explains feature-layer performance, reported in Table 5. Appendix G adds an accuracy–runtime–memory analysis across methods. These substantially extend the diagnostic questions examined; the earlier component ablations, sensitivity studies, normalization experiments, and prediction visualizations remain.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly reports estimated correlations between gradient statistics and prediction error. The seed scheme remains unchanged: 2025 for the main experiments and additional iTransformer results for 2024 and 2026. No increased run count, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds gradient-correlation, efficiency, and PETSA/TAFAS results. Table 10 includes exceptions to ADAPT-Z's superiority: on iTransformer/ETTh1 at horizon 48, PETSA scores 0.3596 versus ADAPT-Z's 0.3626. Existing ADAPT-Z scores also change: SOFTS/weather at horizon 24 changes from 0.1684 to 0.1675 in v1 Table 7 versus v2 Table 8; iTransformer/ETTm2 at horizon 24 with seed 2024 changes from 0.1078 to 0.1066 in v1 Table 8 versus v2 Table 9.

T1.justification: The contextual theorem, assumptions, regret definition, bounds, and proof in v1 Appendix A.3 are retained in v2 Appendix C. The new gradient analysis is empirical, and the computational-cost discussion is conceptual rather than a new formal derivation.

C1.justification: The introduction expands its contribution list to explicitly claim simple feature-space OGD's competitiveness and the frozen-parameter 'learn-to-adapt' phenomenon. Both findings were already discussed in v1 Sections 4.3.1–4.3.2, so this promotes existing findings into main contributions. The central ADAPT-Z and forecasting-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds an interpretation linking stable feature gradients to better adaptation and explains the computational tradeoff between freezing the encoder and computing historical gradients. New Section 5 explicitly identifies empirical layer selection, latency overhead, and limited applicability to simple linear models as limitations, substantially extending v1's qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses prediction batches of 24 and specifies RTX 4090D/i5-12400F hardware for the efficiency study. It adds a reproducibility statement but removes v1's explicit OGD learning rate of 0.000003 and its general RTX 4090 hardware statement. The existing GitHub link is relocated, not newly supplied.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.4 discusses test-time adaptation, adding references such as TENT, MEMO, VIDA, PETSA, and TAFAS and relating forecasting adapters to this literature. This is a focused expansion; the existing positioning around parameter selection and update strategies remains.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language corrections, expands the contribution list, adds dedicated limitations and reproducibility sections, and reorganizes appendix numbering into A–I. Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5 and 10 and efficiency Figure 7, expands Table 2 with existing FSNet/OneNet summaries, and relocates or resizes several retained displays. The author block and conference headers change, while the established figure and table designs largely remain.

improvement.justification: The added PETSA/TAFAS comparisons, efficiency measurements, gradient analysis, and explicit applicability limits improve validation and transparency. The gains are limited by reporting problems: v2 Tables 8 and 10 give unexplained different ADAPT-Z values for iTransformer/ETTm1 at horizon 1, 0.0545 versus 0.0566, and the previously documented OGD learning rate disappears. Overall, these additions provide a useful but limited improvement to the largely retained work.
